Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
- Acute respiratory symptoms (2–3 days) with wheeze, exertional dyspnea, and dry cough in an adult with history of childhood asthma and atopy (hay fever, eczema). Afebrile by measurement (37°C). Not breathless at rest; can manage stairs.
- Most consistent with asthma exacerbation, likely triggered by allergens and/or viral infection (consistent with transcript and DDx).
- Other considerations from DDx that align with transcript:
  - Viral upper respiratory infection/acute bronchitis with bronchospasm (possible trigger).
  - COVID-19 infection precipitating bronchospasm (possible but less supported; no classic features documented).
- Less likely: Community-acquired pneumonia (no fever, no sputum, well at rest), pulmonary embolism (no pleuritic pain, hemoptysis, risk factors; presence of wheeze).
- Conflicts noted:
  - Medication history: Patient initially implied stopping inhalers 3–4 years ago, later reports “normally” using salbutamol PRN.
  - Fever: Patient reported “fever,” but measured temperature was 37°C (normal).

Management Plan
- Salbutamol inhaler: Increase use to 2–4 puffs every 4 hours initially (spacer to be used for improved delivery).
- Prescriptions/Equipment: Spacer prescribed; peak flow meter prescribed. Pharmacist to provide technique instruction.
- Antihistamine: Begin a regular over-the-counter antihistamine for hay fever (specific agent/dose not documented).
- Monitoring: Record peak flow values morning and evening for 1 week; arrange phone review in ~1 week to assess control and consider need for additional medication.
- Safety net: Call back urgently if high temperature develops, wheeze/shortness of breath worsens, difficulty speaking full sentences, or any new concerning symptoms.
- Work/Activity: Temporarily work from home and limit exertion until symptoms improve.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
- Asthma exacerbation (High): Acute wheeze and exertional dyspnea in an atopic patient with prior asthma and current SABA use; limited exercise tolerance over 2–3 days.
- Viral upper respiratory infection/acute bronchitis with bronchospasm (Moderate): Short-duration dry cough and wheeze; common trigger for asthma flares.
- COVID-19 infection precipitating asthma symptoms (Medium-Low): Cough and dyspnea could fit; no typical features reported; measured afebrile.
